name: Fairmont Banff Springs Hotel
label: Banff Springs Hotel
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Bow Falls' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Bow Falls' (node/263386936): point; moved 20 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/24823886: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Fairmont Banff Springs' (329 m across).
notes: The famous castle-style hotel above the Bow River.

text.description: The Fairmont Banff Springs, long known as the Banff Springs Hotel, looks like a Scottish-French castle set among the Rockies. It opened in 1888 as one of Canada's early grand railway hotels, built by the Canadian Pacific Railway. The original wooden building burned down in 1926. What you see now is mostly the 1914 centre tower with the 1927 and 1928 wings either side, built in Rundle limestone with steep copper roofs, dormers and corner turrets. The hotel buildings became a National Historic Site of Canada in 1988. It photographs well because the pale stonework and pointed roofs stand out against the forested slopes behind. Water fills the foreground, which gives the picture depth, and the hotel rises in the distance. It is a closer and usually quieter alternative to the roadside lookout. The angle is described less precisely than at the main lookout, so spend a minute walking along the bank to find a clear line between the rapids and the towers. If you also want the classic view across the river, Surprise Corner shows the hotel at the foot of Sulphur Mountain, with the mountains framing it.
text.geographic_location: The hotel stands near the southern edge of Banff town, close to where the Spray and Bow rivers meet. Bow Falls lies north of the hotel on the Bow River.
text.directions_text: Start from the centre of Banff town and follow the river towards Bow Falls, a short walk. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the rapids and the hotel together. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the towers closer. The ultra-wide (0.5x) suits a close shot of the rushing water, but the hotel will look small.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Bow Falls (east side of the falls, looking upstream over the rapids toward the hotel). Rapids in the foreground with the hotel rising in the distance, a closer and less crowded alternative to the roadside lookout. On the east side of the falls, and look upstream over the rapids. The hotel sits to the south, rising in the distance beyond the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the rapids in the lower third, with the hotel roofs on one of the upper lines. Keep the horizon level. If you want the classic view with the hotel at the foot of Sulphur Mountain, Surprise Corner is an alternative; keep well back from the cliff edge there, as loose gravel is reported.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the hotel to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the pale stone and bright water don't wash out. A Live Photo can capture the movement of the water, and you can choose the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or later in the day usually gives softer light on the stonework and fewer people on the bank.

text.access_note: Bow Falls is a public park area inside Banff National Park, so check the official Parks Canada site before you go for any pass requirements, and check the hotel's own site for anything inside the building.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning or later in the day usually gives softer light and fewer people.
The pale stone of the hotel stands out against the forested slopes behind it.
Exposure can be lowered so pale stone and bright water do not wash out on a phone.
The hotel is about 6 minutes on foot from the stand-here point (straight-line distance multiplied by 1.3, at 80 m per minute).
A Parks Canada pass may be needed in the national park.

name: Banff Gondola
label: Banff Gondola
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OSM W24306232 (Banff Gondola): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Summit viewing platforms over the Bow Valley.

text.description: The Banff Gondola is a gondola lift, and it is the second stop on this map. It photographs well because it combines a clear, recognisable subject (the building and the cabins on their cable) with open scenery behind it, so even a quick snap tells a story about where you are. The phone icon on the map is at the gondola itself, so you can shoot the building and the cabins without walking far. Start with a wide shot to show the building against the sky. Then step in closer for details such as a cabin, the cable and any people nearby, which give the picture a sense of scale and activity. If the cabins are moving, wait for one to come into a clear patch of sky before you press the shutter. Keep the horizon level using your phone's gridlines, and watch for glare on glass and metal, which can fool the exposure. If you plan to ride, the views from the top are a separate set of photos. Check the official site for current access information before you go.
text.geographic_location: The Banff Gondola is the second spot on the Banff map.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot. Use the map to reach the phone icon on the map. Once there, the phone icon on the map is at the gondola itself, so there is no further walk to the subject. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the building and the cabins together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the surroundings and sky in the frame as well. Use the telephoto lens (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out a single cabin on the cable.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Move a few steps back or to one side to find a clear view without obstructions in front of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the horizon and the building's edges level. Include some of the surroundings and sky behind the gondola to show where it is. For a second picture, move in and frame a cabin against the sky with a bit of empty space around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the cabin or building to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the details stay clear. Try a Live Photo or motion shot when a cabin is passing, then choose the best frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go when the light is soft, such as early morning or late afternoon, and aim for a day with some clear sky. Midday sun can bring harsh glare.

text.access_note: Check the official site for current access information before you go.

name: Banff Upper Hot Springs
label: Upper Hot Springs
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Sulphur Mountain Trail' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Lower Sulphur Mountain Trail' (way/1532833704): point nearest the subject (711 m long).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q4854872: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Historic hot spring pool on Sulphur Mountain.

text.description:
Banff Upper Hot Springs are outdoor hot pools on the slopes above the Banff townsite, set in Banff National Park. The water is kept at about 38 °C, the hottest of the Banff springs, and at 1,585 metres the pool is the highest hot spring in Canada. Indigenous Peoples including the Stoney Nakoda and Secwépemc used the springs long before Europeans arrived in 1883. The bathhouse was declared a Registered Federal Heritage Building in 1931.

For photographs, the best free view is from Sulphur Mountain Trail, a short way up the trail above the springs. From there you look down over the bathhouse buildings and pools, with the surrounding peaks beyond. The height lets you show the whole setting in one frame instead of a close-up of steam and heads. Bathers in the pool look across the valley to Mount Rundle, while the trail view shows the surrounding peaks.

Take a few frames from the trail, then walk back down for a closer look at the buildings. If you go into the pool area, you can also photograph the steaming water with Mount Rundle's jagged profile behind it. That area is paid, so check the official site before you go. Keep your phone away from wet hands and steam, and wipe the lens before each shot, because a misted lens makes everything look soft.
text.geographic_location: The springs are on the slopes above the Banff townsite, in Banff National Park.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot. Approach from the Banff townsite by road along the Upper Hot Springs road, which has been open to motorists since 1915, or on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start on the default lens (1x) for the full view down over the buildings and pools. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the pools and the peak shapes. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of sky and slope, and keep buildings away from the edges, where they stretch.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Sulphur Mountain Trail (a short way up the trail above the springs). A higher, elevated view looking down over the hot springs buildings and pools toward the surrounding peaks. A short way up the trail above the springs. From here the springs lie to the west, and you look down over the hot springs buildings and pools towards the surrounding peaks.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the buildings and pools in the lower third, with the mountains filling the top. Include a bit of trail or trees at the edge of the frame to give depth. As an alternative, the pool edge gives a close view of the steaming water with Mount Rundle rising behind it, but that part is paid.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the pools or buildings to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the steam does not turn white. Wipe the lens first, as steam and spray leave a film.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft light early or late in the day usually flatters the mountains and the buildings. Cooler air tends to show more steam over the pools.

text.access_note: Sulphur Mountain Trail is free and reached on foot, but the springs themselves are a ticketed commercial site, so check the official site before you go.

name: Bow Falls
label: Bow Falls
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Surprise Corner' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Surprise Corner' (node/341211830): point.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q37289: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Wide waterfall on the Bow River below the hotel.

text.description:
Bow Falls is a broad, tumbling waterfall on the Bow River, just before the river meets the Spray River. It sits close to the Banff Springs Hotel and its golf course, and it is an easy walk from Banff. That is why so many visitors come, even though the falls are fairly small. Many people also know it from the 1953 film River of No Return with Marilyn Monroe, which featured the falls.

It photographs well because the white water, the river and the mountain backdrop all fit in one frame. There are two good ways to shoot it. The first is the riverbank, where you look up at the cascades with spray and rocks in the foreground. The second is Surprise Corner, an elevated platform above the falls off Tunnel Mountain Road. From there the Fairmont Banff Springs Hotel rises above the trees with the Spray Valley beyond, and you get a glimpse of the falls below. The falls are only partly visible there, so treat it as a classic hotel postcard view with the water as a bonus. The full width of the falls, with the hotel and Mount Rundle behind, is seen from Bow Falls Viewpoint.

Keep your phone steady, wipe the lens before you shoot, and take a few frames at different zoom levels. Drones are not allowed here.
text.geographic_location: Bow Falls is on the Bow River in Banff, near the Banff Springs Hotel and its golf course, close to where the Spray River joins the Bow. Surprise Corner, off Tunnel Mountain Road, is a separate recommended viewpoint.
text.directions_text: From the centre of Banff, head towards the Banff Springs Hotel; it is a 20-25 minute uphill walk to Surprise Corner. There is a small car park there for about 10 cars. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to frame the hotel above the trees. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the water below. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the valley, but the falls will look small.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Surprise Corner (elevated platform above the falls, off Tunnel Mountain Road). The Fairmont Banff Springs Hotel framed above the trees and the Spray Valley, with a glimpse of the falls below. For the hotel postcard view, Surprise Corner is a recommended second viewpoint: on the elevated platform above the falls you see the Fairmont Banff Springs Hotel framed above the trees and the Spray Valley, with a glimpse of the falls below.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: At Surprise Corner, turn on gridlines and place the hotel on one of the upper intersections, with the trees along the bottom of the frame. For a fuller view of the falls, try the second angle at Bow Falls Viewpoint, which shows the full width of the falls with the hotel and Mount Rundle behind. At the riverbank you can look up at the cascades with spray and rocks in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the hotel or the falls to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky and white water keep their detail. Try a Live Photo at the falls to catch the movement of the water. Wipe the lens first, as spray can leave marks.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning, when the sun lights Sulphur Mountain. In the afternoon the sun sets over the hotel, so the light is more backlit. Midday in summer is when the coach-tour crowds peak.

text.access_note: This is an open public viewpoint and riverbank, but the upper clifftop viewpoint is reported closed in winter and paths can be icy, so check the official site before you go.

name: Vermilion Lakes
label: Vermilion Lakes
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Vermilion Lakes Road' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Vermilion Lakes Road nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-17: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).
notes: Sunrise and sunset lakes with Mount Rundle reflections.

text.description:
The Vermilion Lakes are a chain of three lakes just west of Banff, lying in the Bow River valley inside Banff National Park, at the foot of Mount Norquay. They sit between the Trans-Canada Highway and the Canadian Pacific Railway tracks, so they are easy to reach from town. They are also old: evidence of people camping and making obsidian tools around the lakes goes back about 10,800 years.

For photographs, the pick is the shoreline and dock at the Second Vermilion Lake, on Vermilion Lakes Road. On a still morning the water mirrors Mount Rundle, and the dock or boardwalk gives you a foreground that leads the eye towards the mountain. The lake faces Rundle, so the peak catches the first light at sunrise. If you only have time for one stop, this is the one to make.

Start with a wide, simple frame: dock at the bottom, water in the middle, mountain above. Then take a second shot with a tighter crop on the peak and its reflection. If the surface is rippled, the reflection breaks up, so wait a minute for a calm moment. The road is popular with cyclists, so stay off the carriageway while you shoot. Wildlife such as moose and elk can be around, so keep your distance, and expect plenty of mosquitoes in summer. For a higher, wider view of the whole chain of lakes with Rundle behind, the roadside pull-out at Vermilion Lakes Viewpoint is a good second stop.
text.geographic_location: The lakes lie immediately west of the town of Banff, in the Bow River valley, between the Trans-Canada Highway and the railway tracks, below Mount Norquay.
text.directions_text: From the centre of Banff, head west towards the lakes. No station or stop is listed nearby. Vermilion Lakes Road is reached from the Mount Norquay Road exit off the Trans-Canada Highway. The Vermilion Lakes Viewpoint pull-out is another roadside stop. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the classic view of Mount Rundle and its reflection. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the dock to fill the foreground. Try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to crop in on the peak and its mirror image.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Vermilion Lakes Road (shoreline and dock at the Second Vermilion Lake). Mount Rundle reflected in the still water of the second lake, with the dock or boardwalk as foreground. At the shoreline and dock at the Second Vermilion Lake. From here you look across the still water to Mount Rundle, with the dock or boardwalk as your foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the horizon on the lower third line, so the mountain and sky get most of the frame. Keep the dock leading into the picture. For a different view, the calm stretch of Vermilion Lakes Road gives Rundle's reflection with fewer people in the shot, and the Vermilion Lakes Viewpoint pull-out gives a higher, wider look at the whole chain of lakes.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the mountain to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour. Hold the phone still against your body or the dock rail. Try a Live Photo, which can catch a calm moment on the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: About 30 minutes before sunrise, when the lake is calm and Rundle catches the first light.

text.access_note: This is a roadside public area inside Banff National Park, and a park pass is probably needed at some times of year, so check the official site before you go.

name: Cave and Basin National Historic Site
label: Cave and Basin
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Cave and Basin National Historic Site' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/263388342: the OpenStreetMap point 'Cave & Basin National Historic Site'.
notes: Birthplace of Canada's national parks, with a hot spring cave.

text.description:
Cave and Basin is the place where Banff National Park began. In 1883 three railway workers lowered themselves through a hole in the cave roof using a felled tree, and by 1885 the Canadian government had reserved about 26 square kilometres around the springs. That reserve was the start of Canada's national parks. The site was declared a National Historic Site in 1981.

For a phone photo, the best free subject is the outdoor thermal basin. Steam rises from the water in the foreground, and the Rocky Mountain peaks stand behind it. The warm water and cold mountain air make the scene feel alive, and the historic building's grounds give you stone, water and sky in one frame. The springs are also home to the Banff Springs snail, an endangered species, which is a good reason to keep to the marked paths and boardwalks.

The cave interior, with its hot spring pool and the shaft of light from the roof opening, is inside the admission building. Treat it as a separate visit and check the official site before you go. For a second angle, the Discovery Trail offers a higher view of the basin and building roofs, with Mount Cory, Mount Norquay and Cascade Mountain in the distance (confirm its location on the map). Take your outdoor shots first, then decide whether to go inside.
text.geographic_location: Cave and Basin is in the town of Banff, on the lower northeast flank of Sulphur Mountain. It sits within Banff National Park.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram, rail or other public transport stop is listed for this spot. Use the map to reach the site, which is on the lower slopes of Sulphur Mountain in the town of Banff. Once you arrive, the phone icon on the map is at the front of the outdoor basin, inside the historic building's grounds. Follow the signed paths and boardwalks from the entrance. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole basin and the mountains into one frame. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the peaks or the rising steam.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the steaming basin fills the foreground and the Rocky Mountain peaks rise behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the water's edge on the lower line, so the basin leads the eye up to the mountains. Keep the horizon level. If you want a higher view of the basin and building roofs, the Discovery Trail is a good alternative (confirm its location on the map).
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the steam to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the white vapour keeps its detail and the sky stays rich. Try a Live Photo to catch the steam drifting.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light, and steam tends to show best on cold days.

text.access_note: The outdoor basin area can be photographed from the paths and boardwalks, but the cave interior is inside a building with an admission fee, so check the official site before you go.

name: Banff Avenue
label: Banff Avenue
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Cascade of Time Garden' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Cascade garden' (pois).
pin_note: Position from OSM W1285779852 (Banff Avenue): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Main street of town with Cascade Mountain at its end.

text.description:
Banff Avenue is a busy through-street in Banff town. It runs straight towards Cascade Mountain, so the peak sits at the end of the road with shopfronts on both sides leading your eye to it. That tidy line is why the view works so well on a phone. The street itself is busy, though, so many visitors prefer a calmer spot for the same scene.

For this scene, head to the Cascade of Time Garden, near the south end of the avenue on the south side of the Bow River. Terraced flower beds and pools fill the foreground, with Banff Avenue and Cascade Mountain rising behind them. It gives you a softer, greener version of the street view, and the flowers are at their best from late spring through summer.

If you want the classic street view as well, you have two other options. You can stand on the pavement or in the median of Banff Avenue itself, with the storefronts framing the peak. Or you can shoot from the Banff Avenue bridge, where the long view up the avenue squeezes the street together and makes the mountain look bigger. Take extra care near traffic, as cars use both sides of the street. Keep to the pavement or median and don't step into the road for a better angle.

For a good photo, keep the phone level, use the gridlines to keep the street straight, and leave a little sky above the peak.
text.geographic_location: Banff Avenue is a busy through-street in Banff town and runs towards Cascade Mountain. The Cascade of Time Garden is near the south end of the avenue, on the south side of the Bow River.
text.directions_text: Start from Banff town; there is no public transport listed nearby, so the spot is reached on foot. Head for the south end of Banff Avenue, on the south side of the Bow River, where the Cascade of Time Garden is. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show flowers, street and mountain together. Switch to telephoto (2x-3x, depending on your phone) for a tighter, more compressed view of the peak.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Cascade of Time Garden (south side of the Bow River, at the south end of Banff Avenue, looking back north). Terraced flower beds and pools in the foreground, with Banff Avenue and Cascade Mountain rising behind them. Near the south end of Banff Avenue on the south side of the Bow River, and look towards the avenue and the mountain. From here the terraced flower beds and pools fill the foreground, with Banff Avenue and Cascade Mountain rising behind them.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Use the flower beds and pools as foreground and let the mountain fill the background. Turn on gridlines and keep the avenue running straight up the middle. As an alternative, shoot from the Banff Avenue bridge for a long view up the street, but keep clear of the traffic.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the mountain to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps its detail. Try the ultra-wide (0.5x) lens close to the flowers for a bigger foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late spring through summer, when the flowers are in bloom.

text.access_note: The Cascade of Time Garden is free to visit and easy to reach on foot, but gardens and bridges can have seasonal works, so check locally before you go.

name: Mount Rundle
label: Mount Rundle
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-17: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).
notes: The iconic slanted peak above Banff.

text.description: Mount Rundle is the long, tilted mountain that overlooks the town of Banff and, further along, Canmore. It is less a single peak than a small range: it stretches for over 12 kilometres south of the Trans-Canada Highway, with seven distinct peaks. The third peak southeast of Banff is the highest, at 2,949 metres. The mountain was named in 1858 by John Palliser, after the Reverend Robert Rundle, a Methodist missionary. Its layers of rock were pushed up and tilted long ago, which gives the slopes their sloping, stepped shape. That shape is what makes it so good for photos: strong diagonal lines and bands of different rock. The painter Walter Phillips called it his "bread and butter mountain" because its mood and colour kept changing, from deep morning shadow to a warm evening glow. Treat it as a close-up of the mountain's slopes, with the cliff bands, the steep tree-covered slopes and the sky above. For the classic wide view, most photographs are taken from the end of Vermilion Lakes road, about 5 kilometres away, with the lakes in the foreground. That is a good second stop if you have time.
text.geographic_location: Mount Rundle lies in Banff National Park, on the south side of the Trans-Canada Highway, running eastward from the town of Banff towards Canmore.
text.directions_text: From there Mount Rundle is about 66 m to the south, about 1 minute on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the slopes. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more sky and the full sweep of the rock bands. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out cliffs, ridges and the tilted layers.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Vermilion Lakes (second lake, shoreline off Vermilion Lakes Road, west of town). Mount Rundle's long ridge reflected in the still water of the lake, often with marsh grasses in the foreground. You are very close, so the mountain will fill the frame rather than appear as a whole.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the line where the cliffs meet the tree-covered slopes along a third of the frame. Let the tilted rock bands run diagonally. Keep some sky for balance. With the telephoto, pick one section of cliff and make that the picture. For the full-mountain view with water in front, try Vermilion Lakes instead.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the rock face to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the cliffs keep their detail and colour. Avoid portrait mode here; it suits people, not mountains.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Walter Phillips wrote that the mountain is in deep shadow in the morning and takes on a warm glow from the setting sun at the end of the day. Late afternoon to sunset is a good bet for colour; check the sunset time for the day of your visit.

text.access_note: Mount Rundle is in Banff National Park, so check the official Parks Canada site before you go for any park pass or access rules.

name: Surprise Corner
label: Surprise Corner
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Tunnel Mountain Road' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Tunnel Mountain Road' (way/236595963): point nearest the subject (898 m long).
pin_note: Position from OSM N13461324098 (Surprise Corner): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Classic viewpoint of the Banff Springs Hotel with the valley behind.

text.description:
Surprise Corner is a viewing spot above Banff with a view of the Fairmont Banff Springs Hotel and Spray Valley. The hotel sits above the treetops, with Sulphur Mountain rising behind it. The Bow River can't be seen from the raised platform, so don't plan the photo around it.

The platform is the obvious place to stop, but guides describe a better angle a short way further on. Walk a little way up Tunnel Mountain Road, past the Surprise Corner parking lot, to a barricade and small pedestrian area by the cliff edge. From there you see more of the hotel and the valley than the platform gives you.

A few practical points. The parking lot is very small and fills quickly. The platform was reported closed for maintenance in late September 2025, so check its status before relying on it. The cliff edge is loose and dangerous, so stay behind the barricade. If you have time, the lookouts along the Buffalo Street walk give glimpses of Bow Falls and the hotel from several points.

For a phone photo, the main job is to keep the hotel as the clear subject and let the trees, valley and mountain frame it. Keep your phone steady against the barricade rather than leaning out.
text.geographic_location: Surprise Corner is a viewpoint above Banff, with the Fairmont Banff Springs Hotel in view. The viewpoint looks across Spray Valley, with Sulphur Mountain behind the hotel.
text.directions_text: No public transport stops are listed nearby. The Surprise Corner parking lot is on Tunnel Mountain Road, and it is very small and fills quickly. From the lot, walk a short way up the road to the barricade and small pedestrian area by the cliff edge. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the hotel, the valley and Sulphur Mountain together. Switch to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the hotel closer and cut out empty sky. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a sweeping valley view, because the hotel will look small.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Tunnel Mountain Road (a short distance up the road past the Surprise Corner parking lot, at a barricade and small pedestrian area by the cliff edge). The hotel and valley seen from a cliff-edge spot beside the road, which guides describe as a better angle than the raised platform. Up Tunnel Mountain Road past the Surprise Corner parking lot. From here the hotel and valley are in view, with more of both than from the raised platform. Stay behind the barricade, as the cliff is loose and dangerous.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the hotel on one of the intersections rather than dead centre. Let the treetops fill the lower part of the frame and the mountain sit behind. If you want a second angle, the platform at Surprise Corner frames the hotel above the treetops, if it is open.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the hotel to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky looks washed out. Take a few shots at different zoom levels, and hold the phone with both hands.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the hotel and mountain, but take a quick test shot to check.

text.access_note: The roadside spot is an open public place with no fee mentioned, but the platform was reported closed for maintenance in late September 2025, so check the official site before you go.

text.description: Banff Park Museum is a log-built museum in the middle of downtown Banff, and it looks the part: exposed log framing, rustic detailing and a covered wooden veranda. It is a good early stop on a walk along the main street because it gives you a building with real character, not just another shop front. The collection began in 1895, and the building went up in 1903 to a design by John Stocks, an engineer working for the territorial government. It is the oldest building looked after by Parks Canada and became a National Historic Site in 1985. Inside are about 5,000 specimens of animals, plants and minerals from the area. A small zoo once stood behind the museum, from 1905 until it closed in 1937. The wood was restored in 2010 with a clear coating, so the logs look clean and warm in photos. That makes a natural, uncluttered street-level shot, and the building's texture does most of the work. Keep your phone upright to catch the roofline and veranda, and wait a moment for passers-by to clear the frame. For a closer view, the entrance sign and veranda are worth a second picture, with mountains visible behind the building.
text.geographic_location: In downtown Banff, on Banff Avenue, the town's main street.
text.directions_text: Head for downtown Banff and Banff Avenue. Once on Banff Avenue, look for the museum's historical marker beside the sidewalk. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x), which gives a natural view of the whole log front from the sidewalk. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if traffic or passers-by force you to stand close. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details such as the log framing and the veranda.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Banff Avenue (west sidewalk, near the museum's historical marker, looking north). The museum's log facade seen along Banff Avenue from the street, with the town's main street leading the eye past it. From here the photo shows the log front seen from the street, with Banff Avenue leading the eye past it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the building on one side of the frame so the street runs along the other. Keep the phone level so the log walls stay straight. For a close alternative, take a closer view of the veranda and entrance sign, with mountains visible behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the log wall to set focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the sky is bright, so the wood keeps its colour. Take a few frames in a row so you can pick one with no people in the way.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: No best time is documented; the street may be busy at any hour.

text.access_note: The exterior can be photographed from the public sidewalk on Banff Avenue; check the official site before you go if you want to go inside or onto the grounds, as access and photo rules there may differ.
claims_not_in_sources: Banff Avenue is the town's main street.
Mountains are visible behind the museum in the closer view of the veranda and entrance sign.
A sidewalk with a historical marker runs beside the museum on Banff Avenue.
Rules for interior or grounds access and photography may differ from those for the exterior.

notes: Lookout over the town and the Bow Valley.

text.description: Mount Norquay is the mountain and ski area that rises directly north-west of the town of Banff. It was named in 1904 after John Norquay, premier of Manitoba from 1878 to 1887. The ski area opened its lodge in 1929 and in 1948 became the second in Canada to install a chairlift. For a phone photographer, the best picture connected with Norquay is the one looking away from it. From the roadside pullout on Mount Norquay Road, the Bow Valley opens out below you, with Banff townsite and Mount Rundle beyond. A grassy slope in the foreground gives the shot depth, and guides call it the classic view of the town and Rundle. Bighorn sheep often graze on the slope, which can add a lively foreground if you keep a safe distance. The pullout is free to stop at and easy to reach by car, but parking can be full and the area may be icy in winter. In summer the North American chairlift runs for sightseeing, but we have not treated the summit as the main photo spot. Take a wide frame first, then a closer one of Rundle, and check the result by tapping the screen to refocus and adjusting brightness if the sky looks too bright.
text.geographic_location: On Mount Norquay Road, on the slopes north-west of the town of Banff, with the pullout about 4.8 km up the road from town. The Mount Norquay resort lies just to the north.
text.directions_text: From the town of Banff, head up Mount Norquay Road; it is easy to reach by car. Look for the pullout with the grassy slope (the 'Green Spot') on the right, about 4.8 km up from town, below the cement barrier, and confirm its position on the map. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the town, the valley and Mount Rundle together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the grassy slope in the foreground. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out Rundle's ridge or to photograph sheep from a distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Mount Norquay Road (Pullout with a grassy slope (the 'Green Spot') on the right, about 4.8 km up the road from town, below the cement barrier). Banff townsite and Mount Rundle, with the Bow Valley spread out below, framed from a grassy foreground. From here the view looks out over Banff townsite and Mount Rundle, with the Bow Valley spread out below. The Mount Norquay slopes rise to the north, behind you as you face the view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the upper or lower third line. Keep some of the grass at the bottom of the frame as a foreground. Take one wide shot of the whole valley and one tighter shot of Rundle.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the town to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour near sunset. If bighorn sheep are present, stay well back and use the telephoto lens rather than walking closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Guides recommend the afternoon through to sunset, and one also suggests sunrise.

text.access_note: The roadside pullout is a public stop; parking can be full and may be icy in winter, and the chairlift and resort areas are separate, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Looking out from the pullout towards Banff and Mount Rundle means facing roughly south or south-east, with Mount Norquay behind you to the north.
Using the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) will include more of the foreground grass in the frame.
Lowering the exposure slider helps keep sky colour near sunset.
